_what: Where an official icon comes from, and in what order. Icons are NOT bundled in this repository: there are 2,693 official cloud-service SVGs alone and they are revised quarterly, so a vendored copy is stale the day it lands. They are resolved on demand and written into the renderer's icon cache, which accepts any name.
_ranking_why: Iconify's own search cannot be trusted to rank brands: `railway` returns a TRAIN (mdi:railway) above the Railway logo, `fly` returns an INSECT, and `cloudflare` returns a pixel-art glyph above logos:cloudflare. So the ranking here is explicit and deterministic rather than a top-of-search pick — official vendor art first, curated brand catalogues next, and a generic UI glyph only when nothing better exists.

sources.name: Official AWS, Azure and Google Cloud architecture icons
sources.what: The vendors' own architecture icon sets, indexed by tf2d2/icons. 1,858 AWS, 619 Azure, 216 GCP. This is the set the reference diagram is drawn from, and the only source that has an icon for an individual cloud SERVICE rather than the provider's corporate logo.
sources.licence: Vendor trademarks, licensed by each vendor for use in architecture diagrams. Not open-source icons; recorded per resolution.
sources._refuse_path_why: A category icon is a section header in the vendor's own icon deck, not a service mark. `AWS End User Messaging SMS` matched `aws/category/64/End-User-Computing.svg` on `end` and `user` and drew a virtual-desktop glyph on a messaging box. When no official art exists the honest answer is the capability glyph, not the nearest picture.

sources.name: SVGL
sources.what: A curated catalogue of modern company and product logos, in colour, with light and dark variants. Higher precision than a search engine because it is hand-maintained, and it carries products Iconify lags on.
sources.licence: Company trademarks, published for identification use. Recorded per resolution.

sources.name: Iconify
sources.what: 300,000+ icons across 200+ open-source sets, one public API. The long tail: anything the two catalogues above do not carry.
sources.prefer_prefixes_why: `logos`, `thesvg-color` and `devicon` are full-colour brand marks. `simple-icons` is authentic artwork but paints with `fill="currentColor"`, so it renders FLAT MONOCHROME — it sits last, below every colour set, and is reached only when nothing coloured matches. Everything else is a UI glyph set whose `railway` is a train.
sources.licence: Varies by set; recorded per resolution.
sources.prefer_suffix_why: Brand sets carry both a lockup and a square mark: `logos:supabase` has a viewBox of 512x99 — 5.17:1 — while `logos:supabase-icon` is 0.97:1. Dropped into a 50px icon slot the lockup renders as an illegible sliver, which is what the first diagrams using real brand art looked like.
sources._allow_prefixes_why: An ALLOW list, not a deny list. Iconify indexes 300,000 icons across 200+ sets and only a handful of them are brand catalogues; the rest are UI glyph sets whose names collide with product words. Denying the ones that had embarrassed us was whack-a-mole — `mdi:railway` for Railway, then `bytesize:end` for `AWS End User Messaging SMS` — and each new one was found by a client looking at a diagram. A product either has a brand mark in a brand catalogue or it has none, and F1 says what happens then: the capability's own outline glyph, never a substitute.

stale_why: A resolution is a URL and a date. Vendors revise their icon sets quarterly, so a cached SVG older than two quarters should be re-fetched before it goes in front of a client.
_stopwords_why: Noise words in a service label. 'Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL' has to find 'Amazon-RDS.svg', and 'for' must not count against it.

aliases._what: Abbreviations the vendors do not use in their own file names. AWS publishes 'Amazon-Simple-Storage-Service.svg', never 'S3', so a lookup for the name everybody actually says finds nothing at all without this table. Data, not code: a new abbreviation is a line here.

_min_score_why: A floor under what counts as a match. Below it the resolver returns nothing and the caller draws the capability's own glyph. Measured against real misses: 'machines static or ssr' matched an ARCADE GAME at 69, 'uptime crons' a generic app icon at 92, and 'auth orgs' the Auth.js logo at 102 — a different company's brand on someone else's box. Correct resolutions in the same run scored 120 to 162.
_max_aspect_why: A candidate wider than this is a wordmark. The top-ranked SVG is measured before it is accepted and the next candidate is tried instead — name heuristics alone miss the brands that publish no square variant at all.
_require_head_token_why: The first identifying word of a service name must appear in the candidate. Without it a single shared word is enough to win: 'Stripe Connect Express + Stripe Billing' matched AWS's `Amazon-Connect.svg` at 118 against a floor of 110 — one company's logo on another company's box, which is exactly the defect the floor was supposed to stop. Coverage says how much of the name matched; this says WHICH part had to.
_generic_heads_why: Narrowing a name that matched nothing to its head word is safe only when that word names a product. `Celery worker + beat` narrows to `Celery`; `AWS End User Messaging SMS` must not narrow to `end`.
_wordmark_aspect_why: Some brands publish no square mark at all — Stripe's only official art is a 2.39:1 lockup. A coloured lockup up to this ratio is still the official branded icon and beats a monochrome square; past it (`logos:supabase` is 5.17:1) it is an illegible sliver and the square monochrome mark wins. The ladder is: coloured and square, coloured lockup, monochrome and square, then whatever measured.
_colour_why: Whether an icon has colour of its own is MEASURED from the paint values in the SVG, not guessed from its set: `simple-icons:celery` and `thesvg-color:celery` are the same artwork, and only one of them is green. Greyscale paints do not count as colour — a brand mark hardcoded to #000 renders as the same flat line-art as `currentColor`.
_reject_aspect_why: Past this a candidate is a strip rather than an icon and is refused outright, so the component draws its capability glyph instead. Without the ceiling the widest thing that matched was still accepted for want of anything better: `thesvg-color:ping-identity` at 5.73:1.
